messages.body_plain:
> The chi-square difference was significant, but is sensitive to sample size.

Yes, that is called "power", and it always increases with sample size, given that the null hypothesis is false.  That is what you want a statistical test to do.

> Therefore global fit statistics are considered.

chi-squared is a global fit statistic.  Are you referring to fit indices, which have unknown statistical distributions and therefore often have unpredictable sampling variability depending on the characteristics of the data and model?  There is little to no consensus an how to use those, despite how many applied researchers cite simulation studies that offer suggestions for cutoffs in the same breath as saying not to rely on those cutoffs because they may not generalize to other situations.

> I conclude that the configural model obtains an overall a good fit, right?

CFI and TLI are high, indicating the model fits much better than the independence model, if you find that information useful in this particular situation.  Without seeing the RMSEA 90% CI, I can only say the point estimate looks good, although I don't really find "misfit per df" a useful criterion to evaluate model fit.

>
> > fitMeasures(configural, selected)
>    chisq       df    rmsea      cfi      tli
> 2043.239   76.000    0.048    0.988    0.983
> > fitMeasures(metric, selected)
>    chisq       df    rmsea      cfi      tli
> 2184.644   83.000    0.047    0.987    0.983
> > lavTestLRT(configural,metric, method = "satorra.bentler.2001")
> Scaled Chi Square Difference Test (method = "satorra.bentler.2001")
>
>            Df AIC BIC  Chisq Chisq diff Df diff Pr(>Chisq)
> configural 76         2043.2
> metric     83         2184.6     147.91       7  < 2.2e-16 ***
> ---
> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
>
>
> But Milfont and Fischer (2010) write that at least one metric invariance must be established before continuing in the sequence of test.

You mean at least one factor loading must be invariant?  Well, you need at least 2 to be invariant in order to test whether they are invariant.  If there is only 1, you had simply better be lucky.  If you identify the model by fixing the first factor loading to 1, that loading is already fixed to equality across groups, but it is only the configural model (equivalent fit if you free all loadings and fix factor variances).  So you need at least one more constraint to establish metric invariance.

 https://doi.org/10.1086/209528

> I have used the Modification Indices to identify which prarameters should be set free (have different loadings across groups).

The modificationIndices() function only returns indices for parameters that are fixed to a certain value (e.g., zero).  If you want indices to test equality constraints, use the lavTestScore() function.  You can compare the constraints in the output to those in the parTable() or summary() output to see how to adjust your syntax.

> The global fit statistics fit well for the configural model with one free loading. But Chi-square statistic is significan, wich i claim is due to the large samle size (22626 obs).

Due to large sample size AND the null hypothesis of invariance being false, given your distributional assumptions are met.

> CFI has 0 difference.

It has a .001 difference, but what does that mean?  Simulation studies have offered naïve cutoffs being valid based on average behavior, but Marsh et al. (2004) <http://dx.doi.org/10.1207/s15328007sem1103_2> showed that their sampling variability is still affected by N, resulting in strange situations like power actually getting smaller as N increases (the opposite of what you want a statistic to do).  Chi-squared shows you clear evidence against the null hypothesis.  The question you are trying to answer is whether that difference is of any practical (not statistical) significance.  Differences in fit indices don't really help you answer that question.

> Is this enough to establish partial metric invariance?

Partial metric invariance implies you can fit a model with at least 2 constrained loadings that does not fit significantly worse than the configural model.

If you want to evaluate whether the lack of invariance is of any practical significance, you could fit models with and without the equality constraints you find evidence against, and see the impact of those constraints on the difference between groups' estimated latent variances.  If the difference is approximately the same across models, then the measurement-parameter differences are not substantial enough to have an impact on inferences about latent parameters.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

If you use the lavaan() function, nothing will be estimated by default except the parameters you specify in the model syntax.  I would recommend that. Hi,

This is a cross post from stackoverflow <https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/280808/cfa-vs-invariance-of-a-test-different-cfi> as I'm not getting much luck there. Please delete if its not appropriate

I am currently learning how to implement CFA and invariance of constructs between two groups. My data below has two groups. So my steps are as follows

 - Confirm the overall model works
 - Check if both groups have a high enough `CFI`to perform `invariance` testing
 - Perform invariance testing (Configural, Metric, Scalar etc)

I originally created a CFA on a model and got a `CFI` of 0.9305597.
When I attempted to implement `invariance` testing the `configural` step gave me a `CFI` of 0.9233984

    model.between.groups <- measurementInvariance(model=HS.model, data = mydf, group="school", strict = TRUE)

For the `configural` step I got a value of 0.90 for the `CFI`

My understanding of the the `configural` step is that it just combines the groups together with no restrictions on the model. I'm basing this on my readings of [1][2]. I could be picking up the wrong end of the stick completely though

Should the `CFI` not be the same as when im combining the two groups together to test for invariance?

Below is a reproducible example which you should be able to run if the `lavaan` library is installed (I apologize for the spaghetti code) The table `fit_df` contains the fit statistics

Any suggestions or help to help me wrap my head around this would be great

Thanks for your time

1 - Confirmatory Factor Analysis for Applied Research - T Brown
2 - Latent Variable Modeling Using R - Beaujean, Alexander

Code

    library(lavaan)
    library(tidyverse)

    # Function to find the CFA fit put into a Table
    find_cfa_fit <- function(model, group, construct) {

      rmsea = paste(round(fitmeasures(model, 'rmsea')[[1]],4),
                " CI = [",round(fitmeasures(model,'rmsea.ci.lower', 'rmsea')[[1]],4),"-",
                round(fitmeasures(model,'rmsea.ci.upper')[[1]],4),
                "] p = ",round(fitmeasures(model,'rmsea.pvalue')[[1]],4), sep = '')
      srmr = fitmeasures(model, 'srmr')[[1]]
      cfi = fitmeasures(model, 'cfi')[[1]]
      tli = fitmeasures(model, 'tli')[[1]]
      chi_squared = as.numeric(fitmeasures(model,'chisq'))

      return(data.frame(construct, group,rmsea,srmr,cfi,tli,chi_squared))

    }

    mydf <- HolzingerSwineford1939

    # First Create the CFA model for both groups combined
    HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
    textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
    speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

    # Fitting the model with both groups together
    all.fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939)
    summary(fit_all, standardized= TRUE, rsquare = TRUE)

    # Create a table of fit statistics
    fit_df <- data.frame(construct = 'HSM',
                     group = 'All',
                     rmsea = paste(round(fitmeasures(all.fit, 'rmsea')[[1]],4),
                                   " CI = [",round(fitmeasures(all.fit,'rmsea.ci.lower', 'rmsea')[[1]],4),"-",
                                   round(fitmeasures(all.fit,'rmsea.ci.upper')[[1]],4),
                                   "] p = ",round(fitmeasures(all.fit,'rmsea.pvalue')[[1]],4), sep = ''),
                     srmr = fitmeasures(all.fit, 'srmr')[[1]],
                     cfi = fitmeasures(all.fit, 'cfi')[[1]],
                     tli = fitmeasures(all.fit, 'tli')[[1]],
                     chi_squared = fitmeasures(all.fit,'chisq'))

    # Split by Group to check that CFI is high enough for both groups to do invariant testing
    construct.pasteur <- filter(mydf, school == 'Pasteur')
    construct.gw <http://construct.gw> <- filter(mydf, school == 'Grant-White')

    pasteur.fit <- cfa(HS.model, data = construct.pasteur, meanstructure = TRUE)
    gw.fit <- cfa(HS.model, data = construct.gw <http://construct.gw>, meanstructure = TRUE)

    # Specify the fit values
    fit_df <- fit_df %>%
      rbind (find_cfa_fit(pasteur.fit,'pasteur', construct = 'HSM')) %>%
      rbind (find_cfa_fit(gw.fit,'gw', construct = 'HSM'))

    # Remove the Row Names
    row.names(fit_df) <- NULL

    # Model Invariance to see if its possible to use the questionaire across groups
    model.between.groups <- measurementInvariance(model=HS.model, data = mydf, group="school", strict = TRUE)

    # Add the model statistics to the summary Table
    fit_df <-  fit_df %>%
      rbind (find_cfa_fit(model.between.groups$fit.configural,'All', construct = 'Configural')) %>%
      rbind (find_cfa_fit(model.between.groups$fit.loadings,'All', construct = 'Metric')) %>%
      rbind (find_cfa_fit(model.between.groups$fit.intercepts,'All', construct = 'Scaler')) %>%
      rbind (find_cfa_fit(model.between.groups$fit.residuals,'All', construct = 'Strict'))

    # Retrieve the difference between CFI
    fit_df$diff[5:7] <- head(fit_df[4:nrow(fit_df), 5] - c(fit_df[5:(nrow(fit_df)), 5],0),3)

messages.body_plain:
> I was wondering if anyone could comment on the most appropriate estimator for structrual equation modelling with non-normal and non-linear data?

You can find robust options on the ?lavOptions help page.  The Satorra-Bentler scaled correction for chi-squared is available for non-normal continuous complete data:

lavaan(..., test = "Satorra.Bentler")

If you have missing data and use FIML to incorporate all available information, you can request the asymptotically equivalent Yuan-Bentler T2* statistic:

lavaan(..., test = "Yuan.Bentler", missing = "fiml")

Note that the Yuan-Bentler statistic works fine with complete data.  If you compare models for which robust test statistics were requested, the anova() and lavTestLRT() functions will automatically detect this and calculate the appropriate (e.g., scaled) chi-squared difference test.  Robust SEs can be requested as well, for tests of individual parameters:

lavaan(..., se = "robust.sem")

or sandwich-estimator-style, which also works with missing data:

lavaan(..., se = "robust.huber.white")

If you like the sometimes-misleading Mplus keywords as shortcuts, you can request both in one step using

lavaan(..., estimator = "MLM")

with complete data, or with missing data:

lavaan(..., estimator = "MLR", missing = "fiml")

The only nonlinear link functions available are the probit and logit links for binary or ordinal data, which also require using DLWS estimation with robust SEs and a scaled/shifted test statistic ("WLSMV" in Mplus-speak).  Any other nonlinearity would require special tools.  Because your only categorical variable is gender, it is presumably exogenous in your model, so you can treat a gender dummy code as a fixed predictor by setting fixed.x = TRUE (the default setting).

http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cat.html

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

> > I was wondering if anyone could comment on the most appropriate estimator for structrual equation modelling with non-normal and non-linear data?
>
> You can find robust options on the ?lavOptions help page.  The Satorra-Bentler scaled correction for chi-squared is available for non-normal continuous complete data:
>
> lavaan(..., test = "Satorra.Bentler")
>
> If you have missing data and use FIML to incorporate all available information, you can request the asymptotically equivalent Yuan-Bentler T2* statistic:
>
> lavaan(..., test = "Yuan.Bentler", missing = "fiml")
>
> Note that the Yuan-Bentler statistic works fine with complete data.  If you compare models for which robust test statistics were requested, the anova() and lavTestLRT() functions will automatically detect this and calculate the appropriate (e.g., scaled) chi-squared difference test.  Robust SEs can be requested as well, for tests of individual parameters:
>
> lavaan(..., se = "robust.sem")
>
> or sandwich-estimator-style, which also works with missing data:
>
> lavaan(..., se = "robust.huber.white")
>
> If you like the sometimes-misleading Mplus keywords as shortcuts, you can request both in one step using
>
> lavaan(..., estimator = "MLM")
>
> with complete data, or with missing data:
>
> lavaan(..., estimator = "MLR", missing = "fiml")
>
> The only nonlinear link functions available are the probit and logit links for binary or ordinal data, which also require using DLWS estimation with robust SEs and a scaled/shifted test statistic ("WLSMV" in Mplus-speak).  Any other nonlinearity would require special tools.  Because your only categorical variable is gender, it is presumably exogenous in your model, so you can treat a gender dummy code as a fixed predictor by setting fixed.x = TRUE (the default setting).

messages.subject_clean: CFA vs Invariance of a test different CFI
messages.body_plain:
> My understanding of this step was that it just pushed the two groups together without any restrictions i.e. it just checked if the CFA was good enough before exploring groups. Is this not the case?

The difference between a single-group and multigroup model is the input data.  If you constrain all parameters in a 2-group model to be equal across groups, that should result in identical parameter estimates as the single-group model.  But the 2-group model will result in 2 model-implied covariance matrices (one per group), which are compared to 2 observed covariance matrices used as input.  By contrast, a single-group model will only result in a single model-implied covariance matrix, compared to a single (pooled) observed covariance matrix.  Because that is what fit measures are based on, the df will be larger in the multigroup model because you estimate the same number of parameters but you have twice as much input information.

So to answer your original question "Should the `CFI` not be the same as when im combining the two groups together to test for invariance?", unless your model fits perfectly to both groups, there is no guarantee of finding consistent fit indices between a single-group model fit to the pooled sample or to individual groups, a 2-group model with no across-group constraints (configural model), and a 2-group model with all across-group constraints.  When your model fits only approximately well (or poorly), patterns of inconsistency between the models you are comparing will depend on whether the model fits just as well or better/worse in one group than another, and for incremental fit indices like CFI, it will also depend on how poorly the null model fits in each group (or the pooled sample).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.body_plain:
> All improvements in chi-square are statistically significant - the null hypothesis that the loadings and intercepts are exactly equal in the population is rejected. Therefore the intercepts and probably the loading should not be contrained to be equal across countries...this also means that the latent mean differences for genders cannot be estimated.

Well, not all of them.  But as I said before, the differences in measurement might have very little impact on latent parameter estimates.  So don't lose hope, just compare results between a fully invariant model and the partial-invariance model you settle on (after testing individual constraints).

> I have then applied lavTestScore() function and obtained results that i was not sure how to interpret:

I agree it is not easy to interpret the first time you see it.  Notice the total score test at the top?

> total score test:
>
>    test     X2 df p.value
> 1 score 60.201  5       0

That is the multi-parameter Lagrange multiplier ("modification index") estimating the likelihood ratio test statistic (chi-squared difference) if you freed all the constraints listed in the $uni (univariate) output.  Although it is possible to calculate the multi-parameter statistic, it does not necessarily correspond to a sensible test.  In this example, freeing all 5 of these constraints would result in a model that is not identified, so you should ignore this particular 5-df test.

However, it is also important to note that the $epc output provides expected parameter changes on the condition that you free ALL of the constraints in the $uni output, so they do not correspond to the EPCs that you get in the output of modIndices().  I would not recommend setting epc = TRUE unless you are also using the add or release argument to specify particular constraints to test.  For example, there are 5 univariate (i.e., 1-parameter, 1-df) Lagrange multiplier tests, which correspond to the traditional "modification indices":

> $uni
>
> univariate score tests:
>
>     lhs op    rhs     X2 df p.value
> 1  .p2. ==  .p95.  1.228  1   0.268
> 2  .p5. ==  .p98.  7.752  1   0.005
> 3  .p6. ==  .p99.  1.323  1   0.250
> 4  .p9. == .p102. 43.116  1   0.000
> 5 .p10. == .p103.  4.072  1   0.044

The integers on the left-hand side (row numbers) indicate that they are the 1st, 2nd, ...5th constraints listed in the parameter table.  The constraints themselves are indicates in the lhs, op, rhs columns.  So the first constraint is that parameter .p2. is equal to parameter .p95.  You can check the plabel column of the parTable() output to see which parameters these are, but they are also in the $epc output (.p2. is the v35 loading in group 1, .p95. is the same loading in group 2).  Thus, you can test each of these constraints, one at a time, by using the release argument:

score1 <- lavTestScore(object, release = 1, epc = TRUE)
score2 <- lavTestScore(object, release = 2, epc = TRUE)
...
score5 <- lavTestScore(object, release = 5, epc = TRUE)

Then you can print each test, and inspect the EPCs if that particular constraint were released.  Note that the uni- and total/multi-parameter tests are equivalent because you are only testing one constraint:

score1$test # total
score1$uni  # one parameter

You therefore get an estimated change of how any parameter (e.g., the latent fullfilment variance in each group) would change if that one constraint (e.g., the v35 loading) were freed, which can be much more informative than the only an EPC associated with the constrained parameter itself.

score1$epc

Daniel Obserski has done some work on these, calling the EPC-interest:

https://doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpt014

Just a note on your model specification:  From your $epc output, it looks like your model syntax is not for a CFA, but rather loyalty is regressed on the other 2 common factors.  You need to test invariance using CFA (unrestricted covariances among common factors), not "full" SEM (i.e., no latent regressions).  Also, judging from the parameter labels, it doesn't look like all the freely estimated loadings are constrained across groups (e.g., fullfilment =~ v36 and experience =~ v37 are not constrained).  Is that intentional (e.g., using the group.partial argument)?

> Saris et al (2009) suggests to us 0.1 as an "importnat" substantive difference in effect size estimate... Am i interpreting this right?

Unfortunately, lavTestScore() does not return standardized EPCs, so that criterion does not apply. In your summary(fit.loadings, standardized = TRUE) output, you can see how different the standardized and unstandardized estimates are.  Because you have ordinal indicators, perhaps there is very little difference, so the 0.1 criterion (or something close) might still be useful.

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.body_plain:
> how to go about actually implementing a stepwise regression analysis in lavaan.

There is not stepwise feature in lavaan, nor would it be consistent with analyses of covariance structure.  You cannot compare SEMs with different variables in the model, even if they are parametrically nested in a GLM.  If you wanted to compare specific hypothesized models, they all need the same set of predictors, but different predictor's effects are fixed to zero, so that the models still contain the same variables and can be compared.  For example:

## specify models
mod.full <- ' Y ~ X1 + X2 + X3 '
mod.fix1 <- ' Y ~ 0*X1 + X2 + X3 '
## fit models
fit.full <- sem(mod.full, data = myData, fixed.x = FALSE, missing = "fiml")
fit.fix1 <- sem(mod.fix1, data = myData, fixed.x = FALSE, missing = "fiml")
## compare models
anova(fit.full, fit.fix1)
## since fit.full is saturated, this particular example identical to
anova(fit.fix1)
## but you might need to compare 2 nested non-saturated models, too

> what kind of extraction commands would I need to use to look at Rsquared and correlation coefficients?

summary(fit.full, rsquare = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)

The std.all column returns standardized coefficients (i.e., estimates if all variables had variance = 1), so covariances among predictors will be correlations, and regression slopes will be semipartial correlations between predictor and outcome, controlling for other predictor(s) with nonzero effects.

Your other questions are not really specific to lavaan.  General SEM questions can be posted on SEMNET:

www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html>

messages.body_plain:
>> model.1 [1] "\n # Measurement Model\n cat(left.side, right.side)\n "

The model syntax in lavaan is a string literal. Hence the single quotes.
It is just flat text. It gets parsed by the
lavParseModelString() function (which is called by the lavaanify()
function). Of course, the syntax must obey some rules. The string
literal is assumed to contain formulas with operators like ~, ~~, or =~
and so on. If the string literal contains rubbish like the string:

cat(left.side, right.side)

then it is no surprise this it does not work. lavaan 0.6-1 will catch
this and give a more informative error.

What will work (and I believe this is what you intend to do) is this:

fit.1 <- sem(c(left.side, right.side), data=x, std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)

or equivalently

model <- c(left.side, right.side)
it.1 <- sem(model, data=x, std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)

So all you need to do is to construct the string literal using standard
R functions (you can also use paste, but not cat, as this just prints
the string to the screen). See the R documentation for character strings
for more information.

Yves.

> Second, if I run my analyses in Mplus, I got the somehow correctly pooled CFI's. Maybe not the best argument...

Mplus does not pool CFI, "correctly" or otherwise.  It reports an average and distribution across imputations.  That simply describes variability across imputations, it does not pool the values with that variability in mind.  semTools, on the other hand, tries to do something logically consistent, although there has not been a study showing whether it "works" (I think we would need objective criterion to evaluate that, which may be hard to define for fit indices).  Specifcally, semTools calculates CFI based on the (single) pooled chi-squared statistic -- the same one you see for the test of model fit. Compared to D1 and D3, D2 is a notoriously poor pooling method (sometimes resulting in higher or lower Type I errors than nominal alpha levels, depending on the data), so that might explain why CFI looks weird when calculated from D2 statistics.  Unfortunately, D3 is only available with continuous data, and D1 is only available if you can specify constraints on an unrestricted model's parameters to form the restricted model.  So D1 is not a good approach if you want to evaluate overall model fit.  Of course, fit indices aren't necessarily helpful in that arena either, depending who you talk to.

Instead of relying on CFI, you could evaluate local misfit by using the resid(fit, type = "cor") method, to see which thresholds and polychoric correlations are most poorly reproduced by the model in a standardized metric.

> I also checked the chisq.scaling.factor and baseline.chisq.scaling.factor, respectively. They are identical across imputed data sets. Thus, the naive scaling factor shouldn't be a problem.

That does not get at what I was suggesting.  I was suggesting that you manually calculate the D2 statistic yourself (for both the hypothesized and null models) from the naïve chi-squared values across imputations; then "robustify" those using the average scale/shift parameters; and finally use those values to calculate CFI.  That way, you can verify whether there is a bug in semTools, or whether D2-based fit indices are just not useful for evaluating model fit with multiply imputed data.

Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.body_plain:
> With large sample sizes (say N > 200) and a sufficiently large number of multiply imputed datasets (say more than 20, but this depends on the fraction of missing of information), D2 can have quite comparable performance compared to D1 and D3.

Thanks for clarifying what I meant by "depending on the data."  Admittedly, my advice is based on only a couple studies comparing (some of) these statistics.  Namely, the original source for D2 (Li, Meng, Raghunathan, & Rubin, 1991 <http://www.jstor.org/stable/24303994>) only advised using it as a screening statistic, not to rely on it for inference.  But in a more recent study (to which I assume you are referring, as you are a coauthor), Grund et al. (2016) <https://doi.org/10.1027/1614-2241/a000111> found that D2 did perform well with moderate-to-large N and low FMI, at least in the context of pooling ANOVA results (i.e., testing mean structure), which are models that do not require large samples anyway.

I'd love to see some research involving more complex analyses of covariance structure (CFAs and SEMs) that compare these pooling methods, especially in situations when the statistics being pooled already do not follow their expected distributions (e.g., scaled/shifted statistics for categorical indicators might not be chi-squared distributed until N is very large, depending on how symmetric the thresholds are; Bandalos, 2014 <http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/10705511.2014.859510>).  Even the Mplus technical paper <https://www.statmodel.com/download/MI7.pdf> only looks at D3 (because that is the only one they implement).  If you are aware of any already published, please share links/citations with us (or perhaps you and Oliver are already planning a follow-up study?).  I'd be happy to update my opinion if I had more information.  In the meantime, I'll express appropriate skepticism about D2 instead of claiming outright that it is probably untrustworthy.

The problem is that the CFI and TLI are influenced by the null model, which in cases where the items have low correlations can lead to lower fit. Even when it shows proper fit in other index like RMSEA. This is a reason why I dont like these ones as much. In cases where CFI/TLI disagree with RMSEA/gammahat I trust more the second ones

You can use the semTools function moreFitIndices to calculate gammahat and adjusted gammahat. These as RMSEA are not related to the null model and are more reliable.

You can look at West, Taylor, Wu (2012) for a review of more fit indexes. It has become due to practice to limit the report of fit to rmsea, cfi, tli. While there are more options

Dear Yves,

As a person trying to use lavaan within some automated analytical processes I've found it very inconvenient how summary() method for lavaan objects works. In R generally summary() returns an object (typically a list) that additionally has its own print() method to do this nice-loooking printing on the console (or other output stream). And there is no easy way to obtain these nice tables that prints on the console as objects to be used for further operations within R.

So i wanted to ask whether it can be considered, to implement in lavaan this approach to returning (and printing) model summaries that is generally used in R.

Kind regards,

Tomek

messages.subject: Re: the interpretation of the model fit indices
messages.subject_clean: the interpretation of the model fit indices
messages.body_plain:
The West, Taylor and Wu (2012) chapter offers and excellent reference.  I just want to offer another perspective on incremental fit indices.

If your sample covariance matrix had only zero values off the main diagonal, that is, only variances no non-zero covariances, then you could fit any structural model by matching the variances and estimating all the structural parameters as zero.  This thought experiment illustrates the idea that data with low correlations between variables offers less power to distinguish rival hypotheses than does data with larger correlations, positive or negative.  One can think of incremental fit indices as providing a safeguard against overinterpreting low-powered results.  If you have a well fitting model that does not improve much on the null model, then you have not made a very challenging test of your model.  You should think about ways to raise the bar  by designing a more challenging test of the hypothesis.

In my informal experience experimenting with the indices using simulated data, it is not very hard to construct an example in which absolute fit indices like RMSEA look good but incremental fit indices like CFI look bad.  However, it is not as easy to construct examples in which absolute fit is poor but sufficiently better than the null model to produce a favorable values for incremental fit indices.  Your fit needs to be pretty good to remove most of the ill fit in the null model.  So, that might offer a perspective that would favor keeping incremental indices in the mix when evaluating model fit.

The fundamental point on which everyone should agree, however, is that fit is not a unidimensional construct.  Different indices measure different dimensions of fit.  This is why most sources favor a profile of different types of indices rather than selecting one index as the best measure of fit.  However, even those who favor just one number can agree with the broader point that fit measures do not reflect a single dimension of fit.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

This difficulty is precisely the advantage of the Monte Carlo method (similar to the parametric bootstrap method), as pointed out in one of the articles posted on Preacher's site I linked to:

http://quantpsy.org/pubs/preacher_selig_2012.pdf

I'm not convinced bootstrapping is really superior, though.  MacKinnon et al. (2004) <http://www-tandfonline-com.proxy.uba.uva.nl:2048/doi/abs/10.1207/s15327906mbr3901_4> found Monte Carlo had slightly lower Type I error rates and power than BCa bootstrap (which had nominal errors, hence the "slight" superiority description), but that power discrepancy shrank as N increased (and they only simulated up to N = 200 -- how big is your sample?).  Preacher and Selig's (2012) simulation, on the other hand, found comparable rejection rates between the two, using the same range of sample sizes.  The point is just that bootstrapping is not the only tool available for valid inferences, and a couple recent simulations have found that the Sobel test can even outperform bootstrapping:

https://www.researchgate.net/publication/261732700_Small_Sample_Mediation_Testing_Misplaced_Confidence_in_Bootstrapped_Confidence_Intervals

?monteCarloMed

Label the necessary parameters in the model syntax, and you can write whatever user-defined function of those parameters you want to test using the Monte Carlo method.

messages.body_plain:
The code may work (and I don't want to comment on that), but there are
methodological issues with how the whole thing is put together.

1. The survey weights may reflect unequal probabilities of selection,
as well as nonresponse and coverage adjustments. In some projects,
survey statisticians create replicate weights that reflect all of
these adjustments, so that the standard errors that you'd see account
for these. Sometimes, the standard errors would go up, sometimes,
down.

2. Beyond the weights, there are also aspects of stratification,
clustering, and finite population corrections that affect the variance
/ standard errors of the estimates. I pointed out to these earlier in
the thread in my 2015 post. The properly constructed replicate weights
account for these. Without access to the sampling methodology
documentation and supplementary data such as the population totals on
the calibration variables, it is very difficult to get these
adjustments right.

3. Simulating out of the asymptotic distribution out of the estimates
produced by lavaan() is all nice, but it does not really get the
benefits of the bootstrap out of the original data such as more
accurate confidence intervals. It is probably a step in the right
direction, but only about a third of the way. (I am pleasantly
surprised by the results in Preacher and Selig 2012 simulation study,
though.)

4. Taking 20 thousands replicates delivers as much on getting
asymmetry of the mediation effect estimates as it does on uncovering
the biases of the simulation out of the asymptotic distribution of the
original estimates as the method. (No method is unbiased, and
introduces its own errors; 20K is enough to drive the Monte Carlo
sampling errors to oblivion, so that any biases would only be too
obvious.)

> Error in solve.default(VETAx[[g]]) :

>    system is computationally singular: reciprocal condition number =

> 8.75384e-18

This means that the variance-(covariance) matrix of your latent

variables (eta) (hence, VETA) is not positive definite. You can check

this by typing:

lavInspect(fit, "cov.lv <http://cov.lv>")

lavInspect(fit, "cor.lv <http://cor.lv>") # correlation metric

If you have a negative variance, or a correlation higher than 1, then

there is no way to compute factor scores.

(the lesson for me is that lavPredict() should check this first, and

complain, instead of letting it fail)

Yves.

I am interested in doing a hierarchical regression while utilising auxiliary variables.

I am interested in regressing a cognitive ability score on age, some control variables and another cognitive ability score.
Let's imagine my regression looks something like this

outcome<- predictor1+predictor2+
predictor3

I have missing data on both the outcome and some of the predictor variables. Some of the missing data was caused by testing errors and should be at random. However, some of the missingness on the outcome variable is related to another variable ( let's call it auxiliary1). Also, missingness on the predictor3 variable is related to another variable (let's call it auxiliary2).

As I said, I intend to do a hierarchical regression analysis utilising the saturated correlated model i.e. inserting a series of correlations between the auxiliary variables and the model variables. So my models look something like this (without the auxiliary variables)

outcome~predictor1+ predictor2+predictor3 (full model)
outcome~predictor1+ predictor2+0*predictor3
outcome~predictor1+ 0*predictor2+0*predictor3

And I intend to use anova to compare the models to each other. My question regards which auxiliary variables I should insert in each of these models. Obviously I have to always include the auxiliary1 variable which is related to missingness in the outcome , but what about the auxiliary2?

Also, in models where some predictors are constrained to 0 do I still have to correlate these variables to the auxiliary variables?

I am also guessing that it is ok to work with predictor variables with missing data in lavaan and it is uniform in how it treats missing predictor variables and does not default to excluding cases with missing data on the predictor variables?
